title: Given a set of intervals each with a start and an end, determine whether any two of them overlap. Solve it with the sort-then-adjacent-check merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Overlapping Intervals (Determine If Any Two Intervals Overlap)

s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by start, then check if any interval starts before the previous one ends; if so, there is an overlap.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Existence check** – a simple yes/no answer: do any two intervals overlap?
- **Sort by start** – reduces the all-pairs question to a single linear adjacency scan.
- **Adjacent check** – after sorting, if current.start < previous.end, they overlap; return true immediately.
- **Touching policy** – use strict < if touching intervals are non-overlapping, <= if touching counts as overlap.
- **Early exit** – return true on the first overlap found; no need to process the rest.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a set of booking windows for a shared settlement channel. Two concurrent bookings of the same exclusive resource would be a conflict. He sorts windows by start and checks each against its predecessor. If any starts before the previous ends, he flags a conflict.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
     Overlapping Intervals: Sort + Adjacent Check

     Input:  [9,12] [13,15] [11,14]
     Sorted: [9,12] [11,14] [13,15]

     Check 1: [11,14].start=11 < [9,12].end=12 => OVERLAP!
     Return true immediately (early exit).

     No overlap example:
     Sorted: [1,3] [5,7] [9,11]
     Check 1: 5 < 3? No.
     Check 2: 9 < 7? No.
     Return false.

     Containment example:
     Sorted: [1,10] [3,5]
     Check 1: 3 < 10? Yes => OVERLAP!
     (Contained interval is detected for free)

     Timeline:
     9    10   11   12   13   14   15
     |=========|         Booking A: [9,12]
               |==========|        Booking B: [11,14]
                    Overlap!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The overlapping intervals problem asks a simple yes/no question: do any two intervals overlap? The naive all-pairs check is O(n squared), but sorting by start reduces it to a single linear adjacency scan. After sorting, any overlap surfaces between adjacent intervals, because if an earlier-starting interval overlaps a later one, the later one starts before the earlier one ends.

The touching policy is a domain decision. For settlement booking windows where back-to-back use is allowed, use strict less-than. For time ranges where touching is a conflict, use less-than-or-equal. The containment case is handled for free because a contained interval starts before its enclosing interval ends.

At National Bank of India, the settlement scheduler validates that no two booking windows for the same clearing channel overlap. Sorting by start and checking adjacent pairs answers the conflict question in O(n log n) time, keeping booking confirmation fast even when many desks submit windows.

This is the lightweight existence-check cousin of the merge-intervals family. Mastering it as a warm-up problem and connecting it to merge, insert, and intersection shows an interviewer you understand the entire family rather than one isolated problem.

Remember one sentence: sort by start, check if any interval starts before its predecessor ends, and return true on the first overlap.

---

keyPoints: Sort by start reduces the all-pairs O(n squared) check to a single O(n) adjacency scan.
After sorting, overlap surfaces as current.start < previous.end between adjacent intervals.
Use strict < when touching is not a conflict (back-to-back allowed), <= when touching is a conflict.
Containment is detected for free: a contained interval starts before its enclosing interval ends.
Early exit on the first overlap found; no need to process the remaining intervals.
This is the lightweight existence-check cousin of the merge-intervals family.
